title: The dry bones (Ezekiel 37)
hook: a valley of bones rattles, joins, and breathes

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem from the ashes of Jerusalem, and rachamim: his mercies are new every morning. Your line was his mercies are new.

Ezekiel was a priest, carried off to Babylon with King Joachin, years before the city fell. He lived among the exiles by a river called the Chobar, a long way from home. That's where his visions came, and they were strange. Wheels full of eyes. A scroll he was told to eat. And this one. The hand of the Lord sets him down in the middle of a valley full of bones. Very many, the text says. And very dry.
screen: `A PRIEST IN EXILE.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, AND VERY DRY.`

segments.voice: God walks him round about them, so he sees how many there are. Then a question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?" It's a real question, and Ezekiel hands it back: "O Lord God, thou knowest." So God tells him to preach to the bones: ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. As he speaks there's a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin. And they lie there. Bodies, but no breath. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, and blow upon these slain, that they may live. Breath comes into them, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The chapter turns on one Hebrew word, ruach. It means breath, and wind, and spirit. Ezekiel uses it all three ways here, sometimes in one sentence, and English has to pick one each time. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel, the exiles saying our bones are dried up, our hope is lost. The vision promises that a people who thought they were finished would live and go home. Christians also hear in it the resurrection of the dead and the gift of the Spirit; the Church reads it at the Vigil of Pentecost and in Lent. Either way, the bones don't argue their way back to life. They're spoken to, and then breathed into.
screen: `CAN THESE BONES LIVE? THOU KNOWEST.` · `BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.` · `RUACH: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT.` · `OUR HOPE IS LOST, THEY SAID.` · then, large: `COME FROM THE FOUR WINDS.`

segments.voice: Let one dried-out thing come to mind: a friendship gone quiet, a hope you stopped mentioning, a part of your faith that hasn't moved in a long time. Don't try to make it live; just ask over it, can this live?, and give Ezekiel's answer, thou knowest, as you breathe. If you pray, pray over it as it is.
ruach. Hebrew for breath, wind and spirit: what entered the dry bones in Ezekiel's valley and made them stand up as a living army. Today's word.
Your line: can these bones live. Thou knowest, Ezekiel said, and the breath came. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones at the Vigil of Pentecost and on a Sunday in Lent, hearing in it the promise of resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

chat.says: What's the dry bones vision in Ezekiel actually about?
options: A promise: Israel's exiles, who said our hope is lost, would live again and go home.
A record of a real battlefield where Israel's whole army was wiped out by Babylon.
A warning that the exiles' sins had left them forever beyond God's help.
chat.meaning: God explains that the bones are the whole house of Israel, saying our hope is lost. The vision promises they will live and go home.

Ezekiel.meaning: a priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon

Joachin.meaning: a king of Judah carried off to Babylon

Chobar.meaning: the river in Babylon where Ezekiel lived

Vigil of Pentecost.meaning: the evening Mass on the eve of Pentecost

notes: The carry 'can these bones live' follows the KJV of 37:3, quoted and cited as KJV; the Douay-Rheims reads differently (roughly 'dost thou think these bones shall live?'). Confirm whether a Catholic-path script should quote the KJV here, or paraphrase only.
Ezekiel among the exiles of 597 BC by the river Chobar (Kebar): confirm.
Ezekiel 37:1–14 as the Pentecost Vigil reading option and 37:12–14 on the 5th Sunday of Lent (Year A): confirm.
The KJV-style phrases 'O Lord God, thou knowest' and 'Ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord' are given as paraphrase, unquoted.
